newsitem.title: HONDURAS: Crash renews debate on Honduras airport safety.
newsitem.headline: Crash renews debate on Honduras airport safety.

text.p: The deadly crash of a U.S. Air Force C-130 cargo plane that overshot a runway renewed debate on Wednesday over poor safety conditions at Honduras' chief international airport.

The Hercules plane burst into flames and smashed into bits upon crashing on Tuesday, killing three and injuring seven at Tegucigalpa's Toncontin airport, widely considered the most dangerous in Central America.
Only the tail section remained intact. An investigation is under way.
Toncontin's runway, built in 1948, is 5,850 feet (1,800 metres) long, about two-thirds the length it should be, according to aviation experts.

Moreover, the airport is situated in the Tegucigalpa valley, meaning planes must make an extremely steep ascent and descent through hillsides largely populated by poor Hondurans living in shantytowns.
As commercial jetliners approach, passengers routinely say their prayers and, after a safe landing, break out in hearty applause and cheers of "Viva!"

"The airport is insufficient, the runway is very short and needs more space," Rigoberto Stefan, a member of a private airport commission and president of the Tegucigalpa Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told Reuters. "Plus, it's in the middle of a highly populated area."

Some have proposed moving commerical flights to the U.S. military base of Palmerola, about 40 miles (65 km) north of the capital, which has a runway 13,000 feet (4,000 metres) long. Even the government recognises the problem.
"It's a permanent risk, but we are a poor country and we don't have the resources to solve this problem," Communications and Transport Minister Luis Zelaya told reporters.

According to the Honduran Civil Aeronautics Directorate, since 1952 there have been 43 accidents at or near Toncontin, the worst in 1989 when 131 people died as a Boeing 727 belonging to now-defunct local airline SAHSA crashed 12 miles (20 km) short of the runway.

The alternative site at the U.S. Palmerola base was built in 1983, a time when the United States beefed up its military presence in Honduras because of Cold War-style guerrilla wars in three neighbouring countries. Palmerola is now home to 500 soldiers, stationed largely to combat the narcotics trade.
James Creagan, U.S. ambassador to Honduras, said on Wednesday that Hondurans were welcome to use the base for civilian flights.
"This is something for you (Hondurans) to decide," Creagan told reporters. "There are different options. It totally depends on whether you want an airport here or there."
